A new report from Counterpoint Research points out that the US budget smartphone market in the second quarter of 2026 has come under pricing pressure due to rising memory costs, with small and mid-sized manufacturers being hit particularly hard, as larger brands are better positioned to absorb the increase in component costs. Details below.

Rising memory costs hit budget smartphones the hardest

According to Counterpoint Research data, the combined US smartphone sales of Apple, Samsung, Motorola and Google in the second quarter of 2026 fell 4% year-on-year, while sales of other brands in the market plunged 45%, reflecting how smaller manufacturers struggled to cope with rising component costs.

Counterpoint noted that smartphone sales under US$100 fell almost 65% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. This situation in turn boosted Samsung's and Motorola's share of the prepaid market, as the rise in component costs narrowed the price gap between their entry-level handsets and white-label phones.

Turning to Apple, the report noted that although the company has kept iPhone prices unchanged in the US, it has raised prices on other products. Counterpoint expects Apple "to raise prices on the iPhone 18 lineup," with some models expected to be announced within a matter of weeks.

The following is the report content:

Analyst Jeff Pu last week forecast a price range of US$1,349 to US$1,399 for the iPhone 18 Pro, and US$1,449 to US$1,499 for the iPhone 18 Pro Max; separate reports indicated that the iPhone Ultra would start at around US$2,500.

Apple reported its third-quarter 2026 results late last month, with iPhone revenue rising 22% year-on-year to US$54.2 billion. The company also warned the market that memory costs and supply constraints would significantly worsen in the September quarter, with a particularly pronounced impact on iPhone, iPad and Mac.
